title: Super bodies join fight against financial abuse
full_text:
The Association of Superannuation Funds Australia (ASFA) and Super Consumers Australia have joined a national initiative bringing together 26 organisations to tackle financial abuse of older Australians.
The Financial Abuse of Older People Action Collaborative includes representatives from superannuation, banking, financial services, legal, community and government sectors, with participating organisations recently meeting for the first time.
Led by the Australian Human Rights Commission and funded by the Commonwealth Attorney-General’s Department, the collaboration aims to drive practical action to better identify, respond to and prevent financial abuse.
ASFA and Super Consumers Australia will participate in its core working group alongside the Financial Services Council (FSC) and Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) while ASIC and AFCA are also members.
The initiative comes as the commission warns that cost-of-living pressures, delays in intergenerational wealth transfer and concerns about “inheritance impatience” are expected to drive a rapid rise in the risk and incidence of financial abuse.
Around one in six older Australians experience abuse, including financial abuse, according to the release.
Age discrimination commissioner Robert Fitzgerald said the escalating level of reported financial abuse required coordinated action across the financial sector.
“Older Australians have the right to live with dignity, be protected from financial abuse, and empowered to exercise control over their future. No single organisation or sector can solve financial elder abuse alone. We must build the momentum for real action in all parts of the financial sector, as the level of reported financial abuse escalates across the nation,” he said.
“By bringing committed leaders together from every area of the financial sector, we can deliver practical changes that prevent it and ensure we are better equipped to respond to it.”
The collaboration builds on the commission’s Financial Elder Abuse Project 2023–2024 and supports the National Plan to End the Abuse and Mistreatment of Older People 2026–2036.
Council on the Ageing Australia chief executive Pat Sparrow said responsibility for preventing financial abuse should not fall on older people alone.
“Requiring older people to become experts on how to protect their financial transactions across complex, imperfect systems is wrong,” Sparrow said.
Commonwealth Bank head of customer vulnerability Caroline Wall said the commission’s leadership had drawn attention to the scale and complexity of the problem and the importance of a coordinated response.
“Conversations have reinforced the significant harm caused by the financial abuse of older people and the opportunity for the sectors to work together on prevention, early intervention, awareness, capability building and system reform.”
The core working group also includes the Australian Banking Association, Financial Counselling Australia, Elder Abuse Action Australia, Older Persons Advocacy Network and Westpac, alongside legal centres and organisations representing older Australians from diverse communities.
Other organisations and community members will have opportunities to participate through a broader network, with further information to be made available on the commission’s website.
